# The Cook's Toolkit

A handful of techniques and terms show up across the whole atlas. Learn them once
here and the recipes will read like shorthand.

## Techniques worth mastering

**Blooming spices.** Whole or ground spices are cooked briefly in hot fat before
liquid is added. Heat releases their fat-soluble aromatics, so the finished dish
tastes deep rather than dusty. Watch closely — spices go from fragrant to burnt
in seconds.

**Building a base.** Most of these dishes start with an aromatic foundation
cooked slowly in fat:

- **Sofrito** (Latin America / Spain): onion, garlic, pepper, sometimes tomato.
- **The trinity** (Louisiana): onion, celery, green bell pepper.
- **Bhuna** (South Asia): onions fried to deep brown, then spices and tomato
  cooked until the fat separates back out.

Rushing the base is the most common way home cooks flatten a dish. Give it time.

**Browning / caramelizing sugar (Caribbean).** For Pelau, sugar is cooked in hot
oil until it foams dark amber, then chicken is seared in it. This "burnt sugar"
gives the dish its signature mahogany color and bittersweet depth.

**Resting meat.** After searing or roasting, chicken benefits from a few minutes
off the heat so juices redistribute. Rice dishes often build this in as the final
covered rest.

**Dum (sealed steaming).** The biryani finish: a tight lid (sometimes sealed with
dough) traps steam so layered rice and meat perfume each other. A clean dish
towel under the lid catches condensation and keeps rice from going soggy.

## A pantry for the whole book

You will not need everything at once, but these recur:

- **Aromatics:** onion, garlic, ginger, scallions, fresh chili
- **Whole spices:** cinnamon, green cardamom, cloves, bay, cumin, coriander,
  black peppercorns, star anise
- **Ground / paste:** turmeric, paprika/smoked paprika, garam masala, saffron
- **Fats:** neutral oil, ghee (clarified butter), and — for several dishes —
  rendered chicken fat, which you get for free from the bird
- **Liquids:** good chicken stock (homemade transforms these dishes), fish sauce,
  soy sauce, tomato
- **Finishers:** fresh cilantro, mint, lime, fried shallots, toasted nuts

## Kit

Nothing exotic. A **heavy pot with a tight lid** (a Dutch oven is ideal), a
**sharp knife**, and — if you buy one thing — a **kitchen scale**. A rice cooker
is a lovely convenience but never a requirement; every dish here predates it.

## A word on salt and stock

Two levers do most of the work in savory cooking: **salt** and **stock**.
Season in layers (a little at each stage) rather than all at the end, and use the
best chicken stock you can — ideally the stock the chicken in your own pot just
made. Where a recipe says "stock," homemade will always beat a cube.

::: {.callout-tip}
## Free stock, every time
Whenever you break down a whole chicken, freeze the backbone, wingtips, and
carcass. An hour of simmering with an onion and a bay leaf gives you gold for the
next rice pot.
:::
